title: Upali the householder
hook: a supporter of the Jain monks changes teachers; the Buddha tells him to keep feeding them

segments.voice: Yesterday: Jivaka, and the monk's threefold rule about meat. Your line: know your food. Today ends a week, with a gift that keeps going.

In the town of Nalanda lives Upali, a wealthy householder and a devoted supporter of the Niganthas, the community of ascetics around the teacher Jains know as Mahavira. His house has fed their monks for years. One day a Nigantha monk comes back from talking with the Buddha, and Upali, confident, says: let me go and debate this Gotama myself. I'll drag him around like a strong man drags a ram by its fleece. His teacher agrees.
screen: `NALANDA. A GENEROUS HOUSEHOLDER.` → `A SUPPORTER OF THE NIGANTHAS.` → `LET ME DEBATE HIM MYSELF.`

segments.voice: This is the fifty-sixth discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the discourse to Upali. The question: of body, speech and mind, which kind of action does the most harm? Upali's side says body. The Buddha says mind, the intention behind it all. They talk, with examples on both sides, and by the end Upali is persuaded. He asks to become the Buddha's lay follower. And here the Buddha surprises him. He doesn't welcome him at once. Investigate thoroughly, Upali, he says. It's good for a well-known man like you to think carefully first. Upali, moved, asks again. Then comes the line this story is remembered for. Your family has long been a well-spring for the Nigantha monks. You should keep giving to them when they come. Upali is struck. He'd heard that the Buddha told people to give only to him and his disciples, and here the Buddha is telling him to keep feeding the monks of the community he has just left. It makes him even more glad. This is how the Buddhist text tells the story; Jain tradition has its own texts and accounts of that time, and the two don't tell it the same way. But the instruction speaks for itself. Changing your mind doesn't cancel your kindness. Old bonds of generosity are worth keeping. Look back at this week: Mara named at the door, the thicket of people, eleven doors, a hen, a bare bone, Jivaka's question, and now a gift that keeps going.
screen: `BODY, SPEECH OR MIND: WHICH HARMS MOST?` · `INVESTIGATE THOROUGHLY FIRST` · `KEEP GIVING TO THE NIGANTHA MONKS` · `THIS WEEK: A GIFT THAT KEEPS GOING` · then, large: `KEEP GIVING TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Think of a kindness you used to give that slipped when something changed, a call to an old friend, a gift to a group you've drifted from, a neighbor you used to check on, and picture them. Notice that the change in your life didn't make them less worthy of kindness, and picture one small way to keep giving. Then rest with the breath.
Upali. A generous man who changed teachers, and was told by his new teacher to keep feeding the monks of his old one.
Your line: keep giving to them. A changed mind can keep an open hand. A week, done.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often cite the Buddha's words to Upali as an example of generosity that doesn't depend on who the recipient follows; dana, giving, is practiced by lay Buddhists toward monastics and toward people in need.

fork.reveal: the Buddha tells Upali to investigate thoroughly. when he asks again, the Buddha accepts, and tells him to keep giving to the Nigantha monks.

what a scholar hears: the debate turns on danda, 'rods' of body, speech and mind; the Niganthas weigh the bodily most, the Buddha the mental, which shows how central intention (cetana) is in Buddhist teaching on karma.

chat.says: If I join a new community, should I stop supporting my old one?
options: The Buddha told Upali to keep giving to his old community's monks.
Yes; the Buddha told Upali to give only to Buddhist monks from then on.
Only if they ask; otherwise the old bond is finished and done.
